title: Gypsum Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gypsum wells have a 71-foot median depth, 20 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $10,600-$19,100.
h1: What to Know About Wells in Gypsum, Colorado
intro_html:
Well records around Gypsum show relatively shallow wells by mountain standards, but the ground is still fractured bedrock and results can vary from one lot to the next. Among 279 permitted wells within 5 miles, 138 report a total depth and 47 report a pump yield. The median recorded depth is 71 feet, while the median reported yield is 20.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for planning, not a guarantee. Before buying land near Gypsum, compare nearby permits, confirm the intended use, and have a driller evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pump equipment and the required water rights.

sections.heading: Gypsum well depth: shallow records, hard-rock variables
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Gypsum is 71 feet. The middle half runs from 41 to 100 feet, 71% of reported wells are under 100 feet, and 25% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest recorded well is 599 feet. That spread matters when you request a drilling bid: a nearby shallow well may not represent your lot if the productive fractures are deeper or absent.

Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 263 wells, with 2 tied to the Leadville Limestone. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells in this local record set. In granite and gneiss, water commonly depends on fractures, so depth can change over a short distance. Ask the driller to review neighboring completion reports rather than relying on an area average.

sections.heading: How much water can a Gypsum well make?
sections.html:
Reported yields are generally favorable, but the sample is limited to 47 wells. The median pump yield is 20.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 107.5 gallons per minute. Seventy-seven percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. The records show 9% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, 15% between 5 and 15, and 0% under 1.

A strong reported yield does not remove the need for a pump test and a review of the permit’s allowed use. Household wells are subject to Colorado rules, including the 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit. A buyer should also confirm storage, pressure-tank sizing and whether the supply is adequate for the planned home, irrigation or stock use.

sections.heading: Water levels and the local trend
sections.html:
Only 13 permits report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is small. Within those reports, the median depth to water is 21 feet, with the middle half from 6 to 66 feet. That suggests water is often encountered fairly close to the surface in the recorded wells, but it does not establish a dependable water table for every parcel.

The permit counts by decade do not show a water-level trend. They show 26 permits from the 1970s, 38 from the 1980s, 75 from the 1990s, 39 from the 2000s, 23 from the 2010s and 14 from the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. Treat static levels as site-specific information, not proof that groundwater is rising or falling across Gypsum.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Gypsum, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity spans several decades, with the largest recorded group in the 1990s: 75 permits. The records include 39 from the 2000s, 26 from the 1970s, 38 from the 1980s, 23 from the 2010s and 14 from the 2020s. A current permit was recorded in 2025, so this is not only an older well field.

The most active drillers in the records are Shelton Drilling Corporation, listed with 37 wells; Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, listed with 35; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., listed with 30. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a company is available for your job. DWR permit records should be checked for construction details, permit conditions and the legal use of each nearby well.

sections.heading: What a new well costs around Gypsum
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss, the drilling model uses a rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 71 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $4,600-$7,100. A finished well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical work, is modeled at about $10,600-$19,100.

That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. The final price can depend on access, casing and grout requirements, drilling conditions, pump depth, trench length and electrical service. A deeper hole than the median can move the bid substantially. Get the drilling and site-work assumptions in writing, including what happens if the first hole does not produce an adequate supply.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building in Gypsum
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported records, but dry holes and weak fractures remain possible in mountain bedrock. The permit data also identify 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 7 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. Those mapped sites do not automatically mean a particular parcel has unsafe water, but they justify a location-specific review and laboratory testing.

Ask for a certified water test before closing or before relying on an existing well. Check septic setbacks, soil conditions, drainfield space and the relationship between the well and septic system. Confirm that the proposed home can be served by the well permit and that any irrigation or additional use is legally available.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Gypsum
sections.html:
Start with the nearest well permits, especially around Dotsero, which is 5 miles away, and Eagle, 7 miles away. Records from Wolcott, El Jebel, Fulford and Edwards can provide broader regional context, but they should not replace parcel-level investigation. Look for total depth, static water level, yield, construction details and the permitted use before comparing one lot with another.

For a new build, line up a driller, septic evaluator and excavation contractor early. Confirm road access for a rig, space for trenching, electrical routing and a location that protects the well from septic contamination. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask the Colorado Division of Water Resources about augmentation requirements. The well permit, not a neighbor’s production, controls what you can legally do.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gypsum, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 71 feet, and the middle half of reported wells runs from 41 to 100 feet. About 71% are under 100 feet, while the deepest record is 599 feet. These records are useful for estimating a bid, but fractured granite and gneiss can produce very different depths on nearby parcels.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Gypsum?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 71-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $4,600-$7,100. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $10,600-$19,100. Access, casing, grout, equipment depth and difficult rock can change the final quote.

faq.q: Do Gypsum wells produce enough water for a house?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 20.0 gallons per minute, with a middle-half range of 15.0 to 107.5 gallons per minute. Seventy-seven percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Only 47 wells report yield, so a test is still necessary.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Gypsum, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from yield or depth alone. Records map 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 7 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory, review nearby land uses and check the well’s construction and septic separation before relying on the water.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a home on a Gypsum well?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, total depth, static water level, yield and permitted use. The local median depth is 71 feet, the median yield is 20.0 gallons per minute and the median static water level is 21 feet, but only 13 static-level records are available. Also inspect septic capacity, water quality, access and any augmentation requirements.
